messages.subject: Use of distsamp vs gdistsamp, and gdistsamp clarifying questions
messages.subject_clean: Use of distsamp vs gdistsamp, and gdistsamp clarifying questions
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I realize that this topic has been discussed previously with various examples of study design, but I'm still confused on how to manipulate multi-year multi-visit data, and which model structure is the most appropriate. I've been going back and forth between justifying the use of distsamp vs gdistsamp, and have struggled with manipulating the raw data to be in a useable format for unmarked.

In summary, I'm interested in looking at if avian species abundances differ between areas representing a gradient of energy development and reclamation, based on various habitat covariates (e.g., percent grass cover, percent bare ground cover, etc). We have 40 point count locations in 3 'treatment' areas. The 120 point count locations were visited twice per year (both within the breeding season), for 3 years. We collected continuous distance data for all points.

I understand that gdistsamp fits a temporary emigration model, and that in the documentation it notes that it is not for multi-year data, but it has also been suggested multiple times for use with multi-year multi-visit distance sampling data:
https://groups.google.com/forum/#!msg/unmarked/VWJfixK6Z2k/OwiDuaeoHPcJ
https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/unmarked/OesoTLrawgE
https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/unmarked/gdistsamp$20multi-year$20%7Csort:date/unmarked/DvliCEn91BI/8VbJrEnPFgAJ
https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/unmarked/gdistsamp%7Csort:date/unmarked/JYKMdoTgfdg/IFvKlxSGtsUJ

Since the birds are relatively territorial, I'm not too worried about sufficient immigration/emigration within year or within the 6-minute point count, so I wasn't sure if gdistsamp was appropriate, although the benefit of having g(0) = 1 relaxed along with the previous suggestions in this group to use gdistsamp for this kind of design has me thinking that it is the best way to approach my question.

Since i'm not interested in differences in abundances between years, rather, just between 'treatments' based on various habitat variables, I note that 'stacking' has been suggested previously. However, I'm not entirely sure what stacking year on top of each other looks like, and thought I had it figured out but am questioning that too. Formatting my data by stacking year on top of each other, having a column for visit number, point count ID (that repeats for each year but with no change to the actual ID), year, along with other covariates (e.g., observer, sky conditions, wind, month, etc), was what I initially thought would be best. However, when pulling this into unmarkedFrameGDS, it definitely does not seem to be correct. While playing around with gdistsamp, I also assumed that numPrimary = 3 for 3 years, but again, since I'm not interested in yearly differences, I was wondering if it would be better to have numPrimary = 6 and treat each visit as extra effort, regardless of year?

Any advice would be appreciated, and apologies that similar questions have been asked in the past and that this may sound like a broken record.

Happy to provide more details if needed.

Thanks,
Natasha

messages.subject: Leave-one-out validation/AUC for occu() model
messages.subject_clean: Leave-one-out validation/AUC for occu() model
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

How have folks performed leave-one-out cross validation to assess the predictive power of their occupancy models?

I have an independent observation that was not used to calibrate my occu() model, which I would like to compare to my predicted occupancy to assess how well the model generalizes. I've been sorting through the listserv and the literature, and gleaned from a previous post that I might not even be able to use traditional AUC for occupancy models since they acknowledge false negatives, and the naive absences are subjected to bias. Is there any way around that? Are there any other techniques/measures for estimating predictive power by generalizing to an outside observation?

Many thanks in advance,
Danielle

messages.subject: Re: Leave-one-out validation/AUC for occu() model
messages.subject_clean: Leave-one-out validation/AUC for occu() model
messages.body_plain:
Hi Danielle,

You could calculate the leave-one-out cross-validated AUC of a model in a way folks have calculated residuals at the site or observation level. Each gives different AUC values, but in the same neighborhood.

I'll first paste a modified version of the occu helpfile to show how this works

data(frogs)
pferUMF <- unmarkedFrameOccu(pfer.bin)
plot(pferUMF, panels=4)
set.seed(10)

# add some fake covariates for illustration
siteCovs(pferUMF) <- data.frame(sitevar1 = rnorm(numSites(pferUMF)))

# observation covariates are in site-major, observation-minor order
obsCovs(pferUMF) <- data.frame(obsvar1 = rnorm(numSites(pferUMF) * obsNum(pferUMF)))

# fitted model
fm <- occu(~ obsvar1 ~ sitevar1, pferUMF)

First, calculate your leave-one (site)-out predictions. This is a general approach using sites/observations within this data set, but you could do something similar with independent data, it would just require the same occupancy and detection covariates (formatted correctly) for the independent sample so you can generate predictions for psi (for each site) and p (for each survey).

# generate leave-one-out predictions (a vector for psi and a matrix for p)
# pardon the looping

nSites = nrow(pferUMF@y)
nSurvs = ncol(pferUMF@y)
predPsi = rep(NA,nSites)
predDet = matrix(nrow=nSites,ncol=nSurvs,NA)

for(i in 1:nSites){  cat('fitting site',i,'\n')
  trainData = pferUMF[-i,]
  testData = pferUMF[i,]
  fmTrain <- update(fm,data=trainData)
  predPsi[i] <- unlist(predict(fmTrain,'state',newdat=testData)[1])
  predDet[i,] <- unlist(predict(fmTrain,'det',newdat=testData)[1])
}

At the observation level, AUC is calculated by comparing your detection vector of 0s and 1s to the predicted psi*p value (this can be extracted from models using the handy fitted() function if not doing it via loocv).

# detection history and predictions in a data.frame
obsLevel = data.frame(dethistory = as.vector(fm@data@y),
                      psiP = as.vector(predPsi*predDet))

# remove missing surveys
obsLevel = na.omit(obsLevel)

# crummy observation-level AUC, as expected from random data
with(obsLevel,auc(roc(psiP,factor(dethistory))))

Calculating AUC at the site level gets a little more complicated; this requires calculating the (modeled) probability of detecting a species at least once on a given site (psi * (1 - (1-p[1])*(1-p[2])...).

# observed (naive) occupancy
naiveOcc = apply(fm@data@y,1,function(x) max(x,na.rm=T))

# probability of at least one detection.
#  This called "D-hat" in Moore and Swihart 2005,
# (I use the same terminology in Sadoti et al 2013 and 2017)
predictedOcc = predPsi*(1-apply(1-predDet,1,FUN=prod))

require(AUC)

# crummy site-level AUC, as expected from random data
auc(roc(predictedOcc,factor(naiveOcc)))

HTH,

Giancarlo

messages.subject: inflating SEs and CIs in a colext analysis
messages.subject_clean: inflating SEs and CIs in a colext analysis
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I am fitting a dynamic occupancy model using colext in unmarked and then used the MB gof test in package AICcmodavg, with some bootstrapping, to find out that my best model had a c.hat ('overdispersion', lack of fit) of 2.12. Now I want to inflate SEs and CIs, for which we can trick-use function modavg:

modavg(list(fm50), parm = 'elev:forest', conf.level = 0.95, c.hat = c.hat, parm.type = 'psi')

However, each submodel (psi1, col, ext, p) has a couple of polynomial terms and interactions, and it seems that the inflation can only be done for the highest-order terms. Is there a way of getting that inflation for all terms in the model ?

Thanks and best regards  ---- Marc

messages.subject: RE: inflating SEs and CIs in a colext analysis
messages.subject_clean: inflating SEs and CIs in a colext analysis
messages.body_plain:
Hi Marc,

in the special case where you only have a single model for which you want to get the CI around an estimate (main effect or higher order terms), you can use the warn = FALSE argument, which will proceed as requested by the user:

modavg(list(fm50), parm = 'elev:forest', conf.level = 0.95, c.hat = c.hat, parm.type = 'psi', warn = FALSE)

However, note that when you have a list of multiple candidate models (the usual case) in which a parameter appears as a main effect in some models and in others is involved in interactions (or quadratic effect), then you should leave the warn argument to the default TRUE value.

Best,

Marc

messages.subject: Re: Lack of fit of pcount models
messages.subject_clean: Lack of fit of pcount models
messages.body_plain:
Hi Laura,

This may be a late reply, but you should probably run your GoF test on your global model. Not your top ranking model or any other nested model. Any fit issues with your most complex model should extend to your simpler ones. Then use the c-hat you get from the goodness of fit on the global model to rank all of your models by QAIC and inflate your SEs of the parameter estimates. Or try a different distribution (ZIP or NB) and rerun the GoF on the global and see if the outcome improves.

Harrison

On Monday, November 19, 2018 at 3:52:43 PM UTC-5, Laura Céspedes wrote:
> Hello all,
>
> I wanted to give and update on this topic and ask your opinion again. Using Nmix.gof.test as suggested I found out that the problem was over dispersion, and this was an issue for all models, not only the top models. Therefore I obtained QAIC for all models in the data set and re-ranked them. I was surprised to find out that the ranking changed dramatically, and obtained different top models (including different variables to the top models based on AIC). My questions are:
>
> 1) Is this expected (radical differences in the ranking)? Should I just use the new ranking based on QAIC instead of the original? I am reluctant to do that because, although all models appear to have fit problems, over-dispersion in all cases appears to be mild (c-hat never higher than 1.6, usually around 1.3). However, I do think that adjustments of some kind are warranted because predictions from this models are not at all reasonable (too high).
> 2) About pos-hoc adjustments. Other than the SE, what other parameters should I adjust multiplying by c-hat? I did not fully understand what Sean refer to as my 'parameter of interest'. I mean, I want to obtain predictions of abundance (e.g. using predict), that would make it my parameter of interest? Or should I adjust detection?
>
> I really appreciate your opinions and insights. Thank you all in advance for your time.
>
> Best,
>
> Laura
>
>
> El martes, 13 de noviembre de 2018, 17:38:29 (UTC-5), Laura Céspedes escribió:
> > Thank you very much John and Sean. I figured I had to do something but did not know what. It is the first time I encounter this issue with my data. I will follow your suggestions, thanks again!
> >
> > Best,
> >
> > Laura
> >
> > El martes, 13 de noviembre de 2018, 10:55:53 (UTC-5), John Clare escribió:
> > > Only detail I'd add is that instead of a call to mb.gof.test, maybe Nmix.gof.test instead, and that you shouldn't need to refit anything (rather, make post-hoc adjustments to SE and information criterion). I think there are several posts on the list that discuss what levels of over or underdispersion are annoying vs. seriously problematic, etc, but a few more recent efforts(e.g., here <https://www.biorxiv.org/content/biorxiv/early/2017/09/27/194340.full.pdf>, here <https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0304380018300607>) might provide a little more insight into whether the fitted model produces really problematic estimates.
> > >
> > > John
> > >
> > >

Hi this might be a bit off topic, but is anyone aware of efforts to "combine" the results of presence only models and occupancy models in an "ensemble" modeling framework?  What does combine mean?  Whatever you think it means..

I found two papers in the literature, but neither are particularly statistical........

Albanese et al. 2013.  Using occupancy and species distribution models to assess the conservation status and habitat use of the goldline darter (Percina aurolineata) in Georgia, USA Ecology of Freshwater Fish 2014: 23: 347–359

Peterman et al. 2013 Using species distribution and occupancy modeling to guide survey efforts and assess species status. Journal for Nature Conservation.

I'm not saying it's a good idea to combine the two types of models just want to know if anyone;s done it well. Who and why are we doing this?  long story has to do with bats.
Thanks,

Robin

messages.subject: N-mix study design question - truncate maximum possible count in field?
messages.subject_clean: N-mix study design question - truncate maximum possible count in field?
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I'm working on revising an inherited protocol for monitoring amphibian breeding in vernal pools, specifically counts of egg masses.  Previously, "counts" have been binned into None (0), Low (1-10), Medium (11-50) or High (>50).  I'd like to move towards an N-mix modeling framework (using pcount and eventually pcountOpen) with repeated counts within a closed season.  Often pools have egg mass counts ranging from 0 to tens, but some pools may have many hundreds of egg masses, to the point where counting them becomes impractical given our staff capacity and limited time window for a closed season.

My question is, what would be the statistical effect of stopping counts at a certain number, say, 50 or 100 egg masses, on N-mix model results and interpretation?  I have a mind to run some simulations as oft recommended by the gurus, simulating a population, sampling it, and then truncating counts >50 to 50 before running some models.  But, I'm having trouble thinking through the hypothetical ramifications of this type of data and how one would interpret estimated lambda.  I looked through old posts but haven't found anyone posting this type of situation - has anyone tackled this before?

Thanks,
Alex

messages.body_plain:
Dear Ian,

this might be a super late answer, but is at the same time linked to a question. I had exactly the same question issue in my abundance analysis. I have also 42 sites and wanted to estimate abundance for each site, but given very low numbers of detections per site per survey, i needed a global estimate of detection probability. At the end I decided to go for programm Distance. I used my predictors of detection probability, which were site specific, to get a global detection probability pooling together the entire dataset. Then,the value of the estimate of global detection probability is entered into the model for density as the only predictor for detection. It worked perfectly.

Now, my question is: did you manage to do this in Unmarked? I am now doing analysis of occupancy in unmarked.
